name: MCP Database Servers
title: MCP Database Servers
answer: Model Context Protocol servers expose a database to an AI assistant as a set of tools, such as listing tables, describing a schema and running a query. This site's MCP directory tracks active servers, including many for PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and cloud warehouses. The topic sits inside AI and SQL, where the assistant no longer guesses at a schema but asks the database what it contains. A server of this kind is the bridge between a language model and a live store of records.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: An MCP database server runs as a local process or a hosted service that the assistant connects to over the protocol. It holds a connection to the database, usually through the same driver or client library any application would use, and it needs credentials with the read or write rights its tools require. For cloud warehouses the connection may pass through the provider's own API and authentication. The server itself is small, but it inherits the latency, cost and availability of the database behind it.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The server publishes a small set of tools, typically schema listing, table description and query execution, and the assistant chooses among them during a conversation. A query tool usually accepts SQL text and returns rows, sometimes with a row limit or a timeout to keep a stray request from running away. Some servers add guardrails such as read only mode, allow lists of tables or statement parsing before execution. The assistant sees the tool result as text or structured data and reasons over it in the next turn.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main questions are who the database credentials belong to and what those credentials are allowed to do. A server that can run arbitrary SQL can read, change or drop data, so teams commonly scope it to a read only account, a replica or a restricted schema. Query logs and audit trails matter because the assistant's requests arrive as ordinary database traffic. Provenance of the server code itself also counts, since a third party package holds a live connection to production data.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Work in this area is moving toward finer controls on what a query tool may touch, with row limits, cost estimates and approval steps before execution. More servers are adding schema aware hints so the assistant writes better SQL on the first attempt. The line between an MCP server and a database's own API is blurring as vendors ship their own connectors. The open question is how much autonomy a query tool should have when the data behind it is real.
